title: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Forms existing in larger numbers have a better chance in any given period of presenting favourable variations for natural selection, so they are improved faster and supplant the less numerous intermediate varieties between them.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For forms existing in larger numbers will always have a better chance, within any given period, of presenting further favourable variations for natural selection to seize on, than will the rarer forms which exist in lesser numbers.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.”. Scope: varieties and incipient species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Each component has standard measurements and experimental systems can test the causal chain. Existing public data seldom contain the entire process in natural incipient species.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track common endpoint and rare intermediate populations for beneficial mutation supply, adaptive response and subsequent replacement. Faster adaptation proportional to population size followed by decline of intermediates supports the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Few datasets jointly observe mutation supply, adaptation and competitive replacement.

Rare populations differ from common ones in habitat, gene flow and drift.

fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.38

discriminating power: 0.52
data existence: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism ties three processes, more variation in common forms, faster improvement, and replacement of rare intermediates, and only proxies exist for each. Genomic rates and abundance series can be joined for a modest set of taxa. Because improvement is hard to score independently of replacement, a positive correlation is only weakly discriminating.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate the rate of adaptive substitution or phenotypic change to abundance, and test whether more abundant forms replace rarer intermediate ones in time series and fossils. Faster adaptive change in common forms, followed by decline of the intermediates, would support the claim; evolutionary rate independent of abundance would refute the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Abundance and Ne are poorly known for the incipient species in question.

Fossil occupancy confounds true commonness with sampling.

Improvement is inferred from later success, which repeats the pattern to be explained.
